What do you guys think about TPP/TTIP?

Well, for Australia, the fear is that it will bring the nasty copyright and patent policy of the United States (which was shaped by corporations) to us as well. Not to mention a theoretical increase in pharmaceutical costs as United States drug company's will be able to sue the government and stop its price capping law on drugs.

I disagree with it completely, especially the ISDS provisions. Corporations being able to sue the government for something as vague as "Impeding future profits" is absolutely INSANE. I think it's just become a complete joke to the people pushing this bill. They're tired of turning up the heat so slowly, when nobody seems to care. Now they're just turning it up to 11 because they're so sure nobody cares. We have to fight it at any cost.

It'll be a clusterfuck and generally bad for the populace as a whole, like most of these sweeping plans are. If we could elect people who were beholden to their constituencies instead of their donors, maybe these really bad ideas would stop becoming law.

They have to be stopped. And so do CETA and TISA.

They're all handing power from democratically elected governments to corporations.

Elon Musk is so crippled by his fear of AI, I feel it really hinders him in other aspects of his life. What does he think is going to fly his space ships when the entire crew is in suspended animation during the long flight?

I don't really see where his problem with genetic engineering is. "Hitler problem"? Why is genetic purity bad? Does he honestly believe that if we remove all genetic diseases that the next step is genocide? If we can isolate genes that cause problems and remove just those, we can still retain our human individuality and diversity while not having to worry about a heart defect 40 years down the line.

If anything it creates more of a GATTACA situation, with "natural" births being discriminated against but hopefully our society wouldn't go that route.

Even if you can remove specific "problem" genes, you're reducing the overall gene pool, minimizing vectors for future mutation, and you risk short-sighted decisions having long-reaching consequences.

Some genes are "diseases" or "unclean". Some are just inefficient in a modern environment. ADHD is hypothesized to be an adaptation beneficial for hunter-gatherer societies. In agricultural societies, and cities, it becomes much less useful and indeed a hinderance. But would you want to eliminate ADHD from the gene pool? Many sufferers would volunteer, even without a mandate, to have their ADHD cured or to not pass it on to their children. So what happens down the line when that gene would be useful again?

If we hit the point where we can remove and add genes freely, and choose our own modifications, it may not be that big of a problem, but it will still present moral issues. Additionally, until we reach that point, our best bet for removing a gene will be selective embryo implantation, exactly like GATTACA, which can't control for every sequence but can rule out specific sets of genes. While better than mass sterilization, it's still crude and will lead to unforseen consequences as we bridge the gap to full genetic control.

We should at least wait for full sequencing before we start tampering. There are many questioned that need to be answered before we jump onboard. I only hope no corporations find a way to monetize services like this before we can plan ahead.

But would a perfect human still be human? Should we make people smarter and stronger? Should humans be able to live forever?

Hey, if he wants to "stay human" and skip out on any enhancements, I sure won't stop him, but if given the choice I'd rather get stronger, smarter and longer-lived. And I think I'm far from the only one.

While Pao has rapidly accelerated the decline of Reddit, it's something that I think most people have been seeing coming on for years. As Reddit's numbers grew, the quality of discussion declined proportionally. Maybe it was attracting masses of the "Eternal September" crowd or maybe it was just that the software is not good for large scale discussion. I mean if there are 50 lengthy posts and a few one-liners you're going to naturally skim the one liners first. If one gives you a "hur hur" you might toss it an upvote, and then get around to one or two of the more substantive posts before moving onto the next, of hundreds, of topics. And this process becomes ever more self selective to crap as it iterates through thousands of users and the "hur hur" ends up prominently displayed far above the substantive posts. And of course in reality it's not a few one liners and 50 substantive posts. That ratio tends to be flipped around especially on Reddit.

Ultimately what I want to be different is the users. The supermods aren't an entity in and of themselves. They're a consequence of the userbase of the site. Who in the world is going to want to manage any reasonably large community on Reddit? The numerous mod leaks indicate it seems to be people attracted to it because they can finally have some power and influence over others - precisely the last people you'd ever want in any position of power.
